Area · Core processes

Memory

How we store, keep and retrieve information, why we forget and why we sometimes remember things that did not happen that way.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Memory is not a filing cabinet of exact copies. It is a set of systems that encode information (prepare it for storage), store it and retrieve it when needed. Each memory is partly rebuilt every time we recall it. That is why we forget, mix up details and sometimes confidently remember things that did not happen that way.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

Kinds of memory

  • Sensory memory: lasts fractions of a second and holds a brief trace of what we see or hear.
  • Working memory: the mental space where we hold and manipulate information while using it, like a phone number we keep repeating. Its capacity is small, about four meaningful items.
  • Long-term memory, usually divided into:
    • episodic: memories of lived situations (what I had for dinner yesterday, my first day at work);
    • semantic: general knowledge (Paris is the capital of France);
    • procedural: skills (riding a bike), used without remembering how we learned them.

Why we forget

Hermann Ebbinghaus learned lists of nonsense syllables and measured how hard it was to relearn them as time passed. His forgetting curve (1885) shows a steep early drop that later levels off. We forget because information was poorly encoded, because other memories interfere, or because we lack the right cue to retrieve it.

Remembering is reconstructing

In the 1930s Frederic Bartlett asked English students to recall a traditional Native American story. With each retelling the text grew shorter and was adapted to what felt familiar to them. Decades later, Elizabeth Loftus showed that the wording of a question can change a memory.

What helps us remember

  • Retrieval practice: trying to recall (testing yourself) works better than rereading.
  • Spacing study over several sessions instead of cramming.
  • Making meaning: linking the new to what we already know.
  • Sleep: sleep takes part in consolidating what we have learned.
Level 3 · Going further, with references

The case of Henry Molaison (known for decades as H. M.) was decisive. In 1953 parts of both medial temporal lobes were removed to treat severe epilepsy. Afterwards he could not form new lasting episodic memories, but, as Brenda Milner showed, he did improve at motor tasks such as mirror drawing, even though he did not remember practising them. It was evidence that distinct memory systems exist and of the importance of the hippocampus.

The most cited models are Atkinson and Shiffrin's modal model (1968), which separated sensory, short-term and long-term stores, and Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model (1974), with a central executive, a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad (Baddeley later added an episodic buffer). Endel Tulving proposed the distinction between episodic and semantic memory in 1972.

In education, the retrieval practice effect (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006) and the spacing effect are among the most replicated findings. Research on eyewitness testimony has changed police and court procedures in several countries.

Open debates: exactly how memory systems relate in the brain; what happens when a memory is reconsolidated after being recalled; and how far laboratory results on false memories apply to traumatic experiences.

References

  1. Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis. Leipzig: Duncker & Humblot.
  2. Bartlett, F. C. (1932). Remembering. Cambridge University Press.
  3. Baddeley, A. D. y Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. En G. Bower (ed.), The Psychology of Learning and Motivation, 8, 47–89.
  4. Scoville, W. B. y Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry, 20(1), 11–21.
  5. Roediger, H. L. y Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
